items.title: The Looking-Glass Self
items.sourceFact: Charles Horton Cooley introduced the looking-glass self: we imagine how we appear to others, imagine their judgment, and develop a self-concept from that reflection.
items.studyInterpretation: In Cooley's looking-glass self, we imagine how we appear to others and develop self-concept from their judgment.
items.originalInterpretation: In Cooley's looking-glass self, we imagine how we appear to others and develop self-concept from their judgment.

flashcard.front: What is Cooley's 'looking-glass self'?
flashcard.back: The concept that self-identity develops through imagining how others perceive and judge our behavior, internalizing that reflected assessment.

quizQuestion.question: According to Cooley's looking-glass self, how does self-concept develop?
options: From internal genetic predispositions independent of others
Through imagining how others perceive us and internalizing their judgments
Exclusively during adulthood in professional environments
By ignoring external societal cues and social feedback
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Cooley introduced the looking-glass self where we imagine how we appear to others and develop self-concept from that reflection.

items.title: Primary Socialization
items.sourceFact: Primary socialization occurs in childhood within the family, forming foundational emotional ties.
items.studyInterpretation: Primary socialization takes place in childhood within the family and forms foundational emotional ties.
items.originalInterpretation: Primary socialization takes place in childhood within the family and forms foundational emotional ties.

flashcard.front: Where does primary socialization occur and what does it form?
flashcard.back: Occurs during childhood within the family, forming early emotional ties and fundamental self-identity.

quizQuestion.question: Where does primary socialization primarily take place?
options: In university lecture halls and formal corporate training
During early childhood within the family unit
Exclusively through mass media and social networks
During secondary retirement communities
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Primary socialization occurs in childhood within the family, forming foundational emotional ties.

items.title: Secondary Socialization
items.sourceFact: Secondary socialization continues through schools, peers, and workplaces throughout life.
items.studyInterpretation: Secondary socialization continues throughout life through schools, peers, and workplaces.
items.originalInterpretation: Secondary socialization continues throughout life through schools, peers, and workplaces.

flashcard.front: What characterizes secondary socialization?
flashcard.back: Ongoing socialization outside the family in schools, peer groups, and workplaces across adulthood.

quizQuestion.question: Which institutional settings are cited as continuing secondary socialization?
options: Schools, peers, and workplaces
Only neonatal clinics
Strictly solitary study environments
Only genetic inheritance pathways
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Secondary socialization continues through schools, peers, and workplaces throughout life.

items.title: The Generalized Other
items.sourceFact: The generalized other represents the common behavioral expectations and norms of society at large.
items.studyInterpretation: The generalized other stands for the shared behavioral expectations and norms of society.
items.originalInterpretation: The generalized other stands for the shared behavioral expectations and norms of society.

flashcard.front: Define Mead's concept of 'the generalized other'.
flashcard.back: The internalized expectations, values, and standards of the wider community/society at large.

quizQuestion.question: What does the 'generalized other' represent in Mead's framework?
options: A specific caregiver who feeds the child
The common behavioral expectations and norms of society at large
An imaginary childhood friend
A biological instinct present at birth
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: The generalized other represents the common behavioral expectations and norms of society at large.

items.title: Social Stratification Definition
items.sourceFact: Social stratification is a structured ranking of entire groups that perpetuates unequal economic rewards and power in a society.
items.studyInterpretation: Social stratification ranks entire groups structurally and perpetuates unequal economic rewards and power.
items.originalInterpretation: Social stratification ranks entire groups structurally and perpetuates unequal economic rewards and power.

flashcard.front: What is social stratification?
flashcard.back: A structured, institutional ranking of entire groups that perpetuates unequal economic rewards and power.

quizQuestion.question: According to the notes, what does social stratification perpetuate?
options: Equal distribution of all societal goods
Unequal economic rewards and power in a society
Complete randomness in career outcomes
Instant elimination of social classes
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Social stratification is a structured ranking of entire groups that perpetuates unequal economic rewards and power in a society.

items.title: Open vs Closed Stratification Systems
items.sourceFact: Open stratification systems allow social mobility based on achieved status, whereas closed systems enforce ascribed status.
items.studyInterpretation: Open stratification systems allow social mobility via achieved status, whereas closed systems enforce ascribed status.
items.originalInterpretation: Open stratification systems allow social mobility via achieved status, whereas closed systems enforce ascribed status.

flashcard.front: How do open and closed stratification systems differ?
flashcard.back: Open systems allow mobility via achieved status; closed systems restrict mobility via ascribed status.

quizQuestion.question: In closed stratification systems, what type of status governs a person's position?
options: Achieved status earned through test scores
Ascribed status assigned at birth with little mobility
Voluntary membership decided annually
Random lottery selection
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Open systems allow mobility based on achieved status, whereas closed systems enforce ascribed status.

items.title: Income vs Wealth
items.sourceFact: Income refers to the flow of cash or earnings over a period, whereas wealth is the cumulative total of assets owned minus debts.
items.studyInterpretation: Income is the flow of cash or earnings over a period, whereas wealth is cumulative assets minus debts.
items.originalInterpretation: Income is the flow of cash or earnings over a period, whereas wealth is cumulative assets minus debts.

flashcard.front: Distinguish income from wealth.
flashcard.back: Income = periodic earnings/cash flow. Wealth = total assets owned minus debts (net accumulated capital).

quizQuestion.question: How is wealth defined in contrast to income?
options: Weekly paycheck received from employment
The cumulative total of assets owned minus debts
The annual taxes paid to the municipality
Disposable income spent on groceries
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Income refers to the flow of cash or earnings over a period, whereas wealth is the cumulative total of assets owned minus debts.

items.title: Intersectionality
items.sourceFact: Intersectionality examines how interlocking systems of oppression and privilege (such as race, gender, and class) operate together.
items.studyInterpretation: Intersectionality examines how interlocking systems of oppression and privilege operate together across race, gender, and class.
items.originalInterpretation: Intersectionality examines how interlocking systems of oppression and privilege operate together across race, gender, and class.

flashcard.front: What does the framework of intersectionality examine?
flashcard.back: How overlapping social identities (race, gender, class) produce interconnected systems of discrimination or privilege.

quizQuestion.question: What does intersectionality analyze?
options: Isolated single variables in economic isolation
Interlocking systems of oppression and privilege like race, gender, and class
Road intersection traffic patterns in urban centers
Independent genetic lineages
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Intersectionality examines how interlocking systems of oppression and privilege operate together.

items.title: The self is social
items.sourceFact: The self is social. Mead argued that we learn to see ourselves from other people's perspectives. Feedback and interaction help shape identity.
items.studyInterpretation: Identity develops through perspective-taking, interaction, and feedback.
items.originalInterpretation: Identity develops through perspective-taking, interaction, and feedback.

flashcard.front: Why did Mead assert that 'the self is social'?
flashcard.back: Because identity develops through perspective-taking, ongoing interaction, and interpreting feedback from others.

quizQuestion.question: According to George Herbert Mead, how do we develop our sense of self?
options: Through biological instinct that unfolds without social contact
By learning to see ourselves from other people's perspectives through interaction
Strictly after reading formal legal constitutions
Exclusively in dreams during childhood sleep
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Mead argued that we learn to see ourselves from other people's perspectives. Feedback and interaction help shape identity.

items.title: People interpret social messages
items.sourceFact: People are not passive. We may accept, question, reinterpret, or resist the messages we receive from socializing agents.
items.studyInterpretation: People actively accept, question, reinterpret, or resist messages received from socializing agents.
items.originalInterpretation: People actively accept, question, reinterpret, or resist messages received from socializing agents.

flashcard.front: Are human beings passive recipients in the socialization process?
flashcard.back: No. People actively interpret, question, reinterpret, or resist socializing messages.

quizQuestion.question: What does the lecture claim regarding human agency during socialization?
options: Humans are completely passive automatons who absorb every norm without question
People may accept, question, reinterpret, or resist messages from socializing agents
Only adults have the ability to receive social messages
Socialization completely dictates every behavioral choice without exception
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: People are not passive. We may accept, question, reinterpret, or resist the messages we receive from socializing agents.

items.title: Institutional inequality constrains agency
items.sourceFact: Inequality is structured into institutions; individual agency operates within systemic constraints.
items.studyInterpretation: Individual agency operates within systemic constraints structured into institutions.
items.originalInterpretation: Individual agency operates within systemic constraints structured into institutions.

flashcard.front: How does institutional inequality relate to individual agency?
flashcard.back: Individual agency is not completely absent, but operates within structural institutional constraints.

quizQuestion.question: According to sociological analysis, where is inequality primarily structured?
options: Solely in momentary individual misunderstandings
Into institutions, creating systemic constraints for individual agency
Purely in genetic codes
Randomly without any institutional pattern
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Inequality is structured into institutions; individual agency operates within systemic constraints.

items.title: Cultural Capital and Habitus
items.sourceFact: Bourdieu defined cultural capital as non-financial social assets—such as education, style of speech, and mannerisms—that promote social mobility.
items.studyInterpretation: Cultural capital comprises non-financial social assets like education, speech style, and mannerisms promoting social mobility.
items.originalInterpretation: Cultural capital comprises non-financial social assets like education, speech style, and mannerisms promoting social mobility.

flashcard.front: What is Bourdieu's concept of 'cultural capital'?
flashcard.back: Non-financial social assets (education, speech style, mannerisms) that facilitate social mobility and reinforce status.

quizQuestion.question: Which of the following is an example of cultural capital as defined by Bourdieu?
options: A physical stack of gold bars in a vault
Style of speech, formal educational credentials, and social mannerisms
Direct corporate stock certificates
A bank checking account balance
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Bourdieu defined cultural capital as non-financial social assets—such as education, style of speech, and mannerisms.

items.title: Individual Agency vs Collective Resistance
items.sourceFact: Can individual agency meaningfully alter deeply entrenched institutional inequality without organized collective action?
items.studyInterpretation: Questions whether individual agency can alter entrenched institutional inequality without organized collective action.
items.originalInterpretation: Questions whether individual agency can alter entrenched institutional inequality without organized collective action.

flashcard.front: What tension exists between individual agency and institutional inequality?
flashcard.back: Whether individual decisions can dismantle systemic structural barriers without organized collective mobilization.

quizQuestion.question: What core dilemma is highlighted in the study of structural reform?
options: Whether individual agency alone can alter entrenched systemic inequality without collective action
Whether people should abandon all forms of learning
Whether machines have socialized identities
Whether income taxes should be completely abolished
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Can individual agency meaningfully alter deeply entrenched institutional inequality without organized collective action?

items.title: Agents of Socialization Matrix
items.sourceFact: Agents of socialization include family, peer groups, mass media, educational institutions, and workplaces, each transmitting distinct norms.
items.studyInterpretation: Family, peer groups, mass media, educational institutions, and workplaces act as agents transmitting distinct social norms.
items.originalInterpretation: Family, peer groups, mass media, educational institutions, and workplaces act as agents transmitting distinct social norms.

flashcard.front: Name the primary agents of socialization cited in the notes.
flashcard.back: Family, peer groups, mass media, education, and workplace.

quizQuestion.question: Which collection correctly identifies agents of socialization?
options: Family, peers, mass media, schools, and workplaces
Solely meteorological conditions
Hardware components and cloud computing servers
Botanical plant categories
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Agents of socialization include family, peer groups, mass media, educational institutions, and workplaces.

items.title: How to Distinguish Achieved vs Ascribed Status
items.sourceFact: To classify a status: determine if the position is acquired through personal effort and merit (achieved) or assigned arbitrarily at birth without choice (ascribed).
items.studyInterpretation: Achieved status is acquired via effort and merit, whereas ascribed status is assigned at birth without choice.
items.originalInterpretation: Achieved status is acquired via effort and merit, whereas ascribed status is assigned at birth without choice.

flashcard.front: How do you distinguish achieved status from ascribed status?
flashcard.back: Achieved = earned via merit, choices, or actions. Ascribed = assigned at birth by societal categorization with no choice.

quizQuestion.question: What criterion distinguishes achieved status from ascribed status?
options: Whether it is acquired through effort/merit vs assigned at birth without choice
The dollar price tag of the certificate
Whether the status was granted before the year 1900
The physical weight of the document
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Determine if the position is acquired through personal effort and merit (achieved) or assigned arbitrarily at birth (ascribed).

items.title: Resocialization in Total Institutions
items.sourceFact: Resocialization involves radically breaking from prior behavior and learning radically new norms, often occurring in total institutions like military academies or prisons.
items.studyInterpretation: Total institutions strip previous civilian identity to systematically build a new behavioral framework.
items.originalInterpretation: Total institutions strip previous civilian identity to systematically build a new behavioral framework.

flashcard.front: What is resocialization and where does it typically occur?
flashcard.back: A radical overhaul of previous norms and habits, typically in total institutions like military boot camps or correctional facilities.

quizQuestion.question: What characterizes the process of resocialization?
options: Gentle informal conversation between neighbors
A radical break from prior behaviors to learn fundamentally new norms
Purchasing new consumer apparel
Taking an optional elective seminar
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Resocialization involves radically breaking from prior behavior and learning radically new norms, often occurring in total institutions.

items.title: Intergenerational Mobility Rates
items.sourceFact: Intergenerational mobility measures changes in social position between generations; empirical data indicates family wealth remains a potent predictor of adult economic standing.
items.studyInterpretation: Intergenerational mobility tracks social position changes between generations, with family wealth remaining a potent predictor of economic standing.
items.originalInterpretation: Intergenerational mobility tracks social position changes between generations, with family wealth remaining a potent predictor of economic standing.

flashcard.front: What does intergenerational mobility assess?
flashcard.back: The degree of movement in social and economic class from one generation (parents) to the next (children).

quizQuestion.question: What does intergenerational mobility measure?
options: Daily commuting distance between home and office
Changes in social status and economic standing between generations
The speed of internet connections across decades
Physical height differences between ancestors
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Intergenerational mobility measures changes in social position between generations.

items.title: The I and the Me
items.sourceFact: Mead separated the self into two parts: the 'I' (the spontaneous, creative, unsocialized response) and the 'Me' (the socialized self formed by internalized societal attitudes).
items.studyInterpretation: Mead divided the self into the spontaneous unsocialized 'I' and the socialized 'Me' formed by internalized societal attitudes.
items.originalInterpretation: Mead divided the self into the spontaneous unsocialized 'I' and the socialized 'Me' formed by internalized societal attitudes.

flashcard.front: In Mead's theory, contrast the 'I' and the 'Me'.
flashcard.back: The 'I' is the spontaneous, unpredictable, active actor; the 'Me' is the socialized self that internalizes society's expectations.

quizQuestion.question: Which component represents the spontaneous, unsocialized aspect of the self according to Mead?
options: The 'Me'
The 'I'
The Superego
The Corporate Identity
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Mead separated the self into two parts: the 'I' (the spontaneous, creative response) and the 'Me' (the socialized self).

items.title: Cumulative Advantage Process
items.sourceFact: The Matthew Effect in stratification demonstrates that initial advantages compound over time, making it progressively easier for affluent groups to accrue additional capital.
items.studyInterpretation: Early structural benefits accelerate exponentially, widening the gap between advantage and disadvantage.
items.originalInterpretation: Early structural benefits accelerate exponentially, widening the gap between advantage and disadvantage.

flashcard.front: What does the 'Matthew Effect' describe in stratification?
flashcard.back: Cumulative advantage: small initial advantages compound over time to create vast gaps in resources and prestige.

quizQuestion.question: How does the Matthew Effect explain inequality?
options: Wealth is randomly redistributed every 10 years
Initial advantages compound over time, making subsequent capital accrual easier
All competitors start with identical resources at every life stage
Effort has no relation to outcomes under any circumstance
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Initial advantages compound over time, making it progressively easier for affluent groups to accrue additional capital.

items.title: How to Trace the Formation of the Looking-Glass Self
items.sourceFact: Cooley's process unfolds in three discrete steps: first, imagining how one appears to another; second, imagining that person's evaluation; third, experiencing emotional self-feeling.
items.studyInterpretation: Three step sequence: visual anticipation -> perceived assessment -> emotional self-validation or embarrassment.
items.originalInterpretation: Three step sequence: visual anticipation -> perceived assessment -> emotional self-validation or embarrassment.

flashcard.front: List the 3 steps of Cooley's looking-glass self.
flashcard.back: 1. Imagine our appearance to another. 2. Imagine their judgment of that appearance. 3. Develop self-feeling (pride or mortification).

quizQuestion.question: What is the second step in Cooley's looking-glass self sequence?
options: Imagining how one appears to another
Imagining that person's evaluation/judgment of that appearance
Conducting a formal laboratory experiment
Drafting a contract with the socializing agent
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: First, imagining how one appears; second, imagining that person's evaluation; third, experiencing emotional self-feeling.

items.title: Is Meritocracy Measurable or Ideological?
items.sourceFact: Sociologists debate whether pure meritocracy exists in modern market economies or functions primarily as a legitimizing ideology that justifies inequality.
items.studyInterpretation: Debates whether pure meritocracy exists in modern market economies or functions as a legitimizing ideology justifying inequality.
items.originalInterpretation: Debates whether pure meritocracy exists in modern market economies or functions as a legitimizing ideology justifying inequality.

flashcard.front: What is the sociological critique of meritocracy?
flashcard.back: That while framed as a fair system where talent and effort dictate success, it often serves as a legitimizing ideology for structural inequality.

quizQuestion.question: What function do sociologists often assign to meritocracy rhetoric?
options: Guaranteed elimination of all social stratification within five years
Functioning as a legitimizing ideology that justifies unequal structural outcomes
Directly providing free medical care to every citizen
An algorithm for computing corporate dividends
quizQuestion.explanation: Source Fact: Sociologists debate whether pure meritocracy exists or functions primarily as a legitimizing ideology that justifies inequality.

documents.title: Sociology 101: Socialization & Stratification Notes
documents.rawContent:
# Sociology 101 - Lecture Notes
Module: Socialization & Institutional Stratification

1. Socialization Foundations
The self is social. Mead argued that we learn to see ourselves from other people's perspectives. Feedback and interaction help shape identity.
People are not passive. We may accept, question, reinterpret, or resist the messages we receive from socializing agents.
Charles Horton Cooley introduced the looking-glass self: we imagine how we appear to others, imagine their judgment, and develop a self-concept from that reflection.
Primary socialization occurs in childhood within the family, forming foundational emotional ties.
Secondary socialization continues through schools, peers, and workplaces throughout life.
The generalized other represents the common behavioral expectations and norms of society at large.

2. Social Stratification & Institutional Systems
Social stratification is a structured ranking of entire groups that perpetuates unequal economic rewards and power in a society.
Inequality is structured into institutions; individual agency operates within systemic constraints.
Open stratification systems allow social mobility based on achieved status, whereas closed systems enforce ascribed status.
Bourdieu defined cultural capital as non-financial social assets—such as education, style of speech, and mannerisms—that promote social mobility.
Income refers to the flow of cash or earnings over a period, whereas wealth is the cumulative total of assets owned minus debts.
Intersectionality examines how interlocking systems of oppression and privilege (such as race, gender, and class) operate together.

sessions.notes: Mastered Socialization foundations and initial stratification definitions.
